bib.title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; appendix A.4 sample dialogues skimmed.

question: How well do general-purpose large language models (244M to 137B parameters) synthesize short Python programs from natural language, few-shot and fine-tuned, on two new benchmarks?
contributions: Two datasets: MBPP (974 crowd-sourced problems, 426 hand-edited) and MathQA-Python (23914 problems)
Few-shot and fine-tuned scaling results from 244M to 137B, with sensitivity analyses
Human-model dialog experiment: natural-language feedback halves the error rate
Program execution experiments showing models cannot reliably predict program output
Analysis of test-case generalisation, pre-train/test overlap, BLEU and sampling strategy

method.summary: Dense decoder-only Transformer LMs trained on web documents, dialog and Wikipedia (no dedicated code files) are evaluated on MBPP and MathQA-Python by sampling programs and executing them against tests, few-shot and after small fine-tuning. Further experiments cover human feedback dialogs, execution prediction and error analysis.
method.task: natural-language-to-Python program synthesis; program execution prediction

datasets.name: MBPP (Mostly Basic Programming Problems)
datasets.split: 10 few-shot prompt, 500 test, 374 fine-tune, rest validation (90 per Section 6.2)
datasets.source: crowd-sourced by an internal pool of crowdworkers; open-sourced at google-research/mbpp
datasets.preprocessing: Reference code checked to pass all tests under Python 3.6; each problem has a one-sentence description and 3 assert tests

datasets.name: MBPP edited subset
datasets.split: 100 problems appearing in both original and edited sets used for comparison
datasets.source: authors' manual editing and pruning of MBPP
datasets.preprocessing: standard function signature, unambiguous text, accurate tests

datasets.name: MathQA-Python
datasets.source: MathQA (Amini et al. 2019) with DSL programs translated to Python
datasets.preprocessing: kept only problems whose code evaluates to the declared numerical answer, removing 45% of problems

datasets.name: Pre-training corpus
datasets.source: web documents, dialog data, Wikipedia; 13.8M documents with 18.7B BPE tokens were web sites with code and text
datasets.preprocessing: source code files not specifically included

models.name: Dense decoder-only Transformer LM
models.context: 512 token context window noted as binding on long prompts; 1024 also tried

training.objective: fine-tuning of the pretrained LM on MBPP train (374 problems), MathQA-Python train, or execution tasks; objective otherwise not stated
training.lr: 3e-5 for the largest model on MBPP
training.steps: 100 steps (MBPP and execution fine-tuning); MathQA fine-tuned 'for longer', number not stated
training.compute: pre-training energy 451MWh and 26 tCO2e; fine-tuning comparably very small

other.execution_finetune_data: 14 x 374 = 5236 train and 14 x 90 = 1260 validation points

inference.decoding: temperature sampling for synthesis; greedy for execution
inference.samples: 80 samples per problem on the 500 MBPP test problems; MathQA analogous
inference.prompting: few-shot: 3 asserts per problem in prompt; k=3 example synthesis tasks (Sec 6.3), 10 held out for few-shot; MathQA prompt has four examples

parameters.prompt_seeds: 15 seeds (0-14) of prompt example choice, read from Fig 6

other.run_to_run_variance: small run-to-run variance in problems solved (59.0 vs 59.6)

metrics.name: % of problems solved
metrics.definition: fraction of test problems for which any of the 80 samples passes all tests

metrics.name: % of samples solving task
metrics.definition: fraction of all samples across all problems that pass their problem's tests

metrics.name: MathQA accuracy
metrics.definition: percentage of test tasks solved by any sample; program output equals correct answer

metrics.name: Execution accuracy
metrics.definition: model's greedy output exactly matches the string from executing the code

baselines: few-shot vs fine-tuned of the same models
eval.protocol: Functional correctness by executing samples; BLEU shown to correlate poorly; human-model dialog on 50 edited problems, each tackled by two people, max 4 hints

availability.code: MathQA DSL-to-Python conversion notebook in google/trax

prompts.text:
Write a python function to check if a given number is one less than twice its reverse. Your code should satisfy these tests:
assert check(70) == False
assert check(23) == False
assert check(73) == True

The largest models that we consider
can synthesize solutions to 59.6% of the problems from MBPP using few-shot learning.

results.quote:

limits: Benchmark programs are short and simple, and the problems solved are the shortest and simplest.
Models often solve a task with only one or two of 80 samples; performance depends on drawing many samples and machine-checking.
Models cannot predict program output on simple inputs; execution fine-tuning data was small.
Results sensitive to the choice of few-shot examples (Fig 6).
Models are not safety-treated and are not released; weights and pre-training data unavailable.
Human-model experiment is small (50 problems) and preliminary; MathQA explanation results are anecdotal.
No fine-tuning optimizer, schedule, seeds or layer/width details stated.
